cards.heading: Autonomous APs
cards.body: An autonomous AP is configured and managed on its own, like a small switch with a radio. Fine for a few APs; every AP's VLANs must be trunked to it.

cards.heading: Lightweight APs and the WLC
cards.body: In split-MAC architecture, lightweight APs handle the real-time radio work (beacons, acknowledgements, encryption) while a wireless LAN controller handles management, authentication, roaming and RF tuning. They talk over CAPWAP tunnels: UDP 5246 for control (encrypted with DTLS) and UDP 5247 for data. Time-critical functions stay on the AP: beacons, probe responses, acknowledgements and encryption. The WLC handles authentication, association, RF management and roaming.
cards.mnemonic:
Control comes before data, just as C comes before D: 5246 is control and 5247 is data.
Only the control channel is always encrypted (DTLS). Steering the AP is what needs protecting.

cards.heading: Cloud-based APs
cards.body: Cloud-managed APs (such as Meraki) are configured and monitored from a cloud dashboard. User data stays local; only management goes to the cloud.

cards.heading: AP modes
cards.body: Local: the default; serves clients and tunnels their traffic to the WLC. FlexConnect: switches client traffic locally at a branch and keeps working if the WLC link fails. Monitor: doesn't serve clients; scans for rogues and intrusions. Sniffer: captures 802.11 frames for analysis. Rogue detector: listens on the wire for rogue devices. SE-Connect: spectrum analysis of interference. Bridge/mesh: links APs wirelessly. Monitor mode listens on every channel for IDS and rogue detection; local mode only scans off-channel briefly. Sniffer mode forwards captured frames to a PC running an analyser such as Wireshark. Bridge/mesh suits links between buildings where cabling isn't possible.
cards.mnemonic:
Most modes say what they do: Local serves the local clients (the default), FlexConnect flexes and keeps working when the WLC link fails, Monitor watches the air, Sniffer captures frames for Wireshark, and Bridge links buildings.
The odd names: SE-Connect is Spectrum Expert (interference analysis). Rogue detector watches the wire, not the air.
Monitor, Sniffer, SE-Connect and Rogue detector serve no clients. Only Local, FlexConnect and Bridge do.

cards.heading: Switch ports for APs
cards.body: A lightweight AP in local mode only needs an access port: its traffic is tunnelled to the WLC. An autonomous AP or a FlexConnect AP switching several VLANs locally needs a trunk.

cards.heading: WLC ports and interfaces
cards.body: Physical ports: the service port (out-of-band management), distribution system ports (to the switched network, usually trunks bundled with LAG), the console port and the redundancy port (to a standby WLC). Logical interfaces: management (and AP management), virtual (DHCP relay, web auth), service-port, and dynamic interfaces that map each WLAN to a VLAN. WLC LAG doesn't negotiate, so the switch must use channel-group mode on. The DS ports connect to trunks because they carry the management interface and every dynamic interface VLAN. The virtual interface uses a non-routable address (such as 192.0.2.1), the same on every WLC in a mobility group; clients see it during web authentication and as the DHCP server address.
cards.example:
interface range g1/0/1 - 2
 channel-group 1 mode on
interface port-channel 1
 switchport mode trunk

cards.heading: Creating a WLAN in the GUI
cards.body: WLANs > Create New: give a profile name, the SSID and a WLAN ID. General tab: enable it and pick the interface (VLAN) its clients use. Security tab: Layer 2 security such as WPA2 with a PSK or 802.1X. QoS tab: Platinum (voice), Gold (video), Silver (best effort, default) or Bronze (background). Advanced tab: options such as FlexConnect local switching and session timeouts. Start on the WLANs tab: Create New, Go, then enter the type, profile name (the WLC's label), SSID (what clients see) and WLAN ID. A new WLAN stays disabled until you tick Status: Enabled on the General tab. On the Security tab, the Layer 2 sub-tab holds WPA/WPA2/WPA3, the cipher and the PSK or 802.1X; Layer 3 is for web authentication.

cards.heading: Where the WLC runs and how APs find it
cards.body: A WLC can be a hardware appliance, a virtual machine (such as a Catalyst 9800-CL in a private or public cloud), embedded in a Catalyst switch, or run on an AP. A new lightweight AP finds its WLC by broadcast on the local subnet; on a different subnet it needs DHCP option 43 or a DNS name for the controller. High-power APs may need Cisco UPOE or 802.3bt Type 3 PoE (60 W); 802.3af gives 15.4 W, 802.3at 30 W and Type 4 90-100 W.
cards.mnemonic:
On the same subnet the AP shouts (broadcast). On another subnet it has to ask someone: DHCP (option 43) or DNS (the controller's name).
PoE goes up the alphabet: af 15.4 W, at 30 W, bt 60 W (type 3) or 90-100 W (type 4).
